name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Tuesday 22 May 1973

clue.text: Bath visitors?

blocks.note: surface reading: tourists who come to the English spa city of Bath
setter's reading: a bath is a public swimming pool, so its visitors are people who swim there

explanation.walkthrough: The capital B makes you think of Bath, the Roman spa city in Somerset; in Britain 'the baths' is also the municipal swimming pool.
explanation.definitionFit: People who go to the public pool are going to swim, so they are the pool's regular customers.

clue.text: It's pleasant to be moderately successful

blocks.note: first meaning: charming, engaging
second meaning, read as two words: to come out ahead on a few occasions but not all

explanation.surface: A modest success is a nice thing to have.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer into two words and it describes winning a little, not everything.
explanation.definitionFit: Winsome describes a charming, engaging manner, an agreeable quality in a person.

clue.text: An expedient for the needlewoman!

definitions.note: describes what the needlewoman does, read as three words

blocks.note: first meaning: a temporary stopgap solution
second meaning, split into words: what a seamstress does when she sews a simple dress, a shift

explanation.surface: A clever stopgap trick that a seamstress might use.
explanation.walkthrough: A shift is a simple loose dress, so a woman sewing one 'makes shift'.
explanation.definitionFit: A makeshift is something improvised to serve temporarily until a proper solution is found.

clue.text: Are set in order for the Festival

indicators.note: putting things in order means arranging them afresh, so the preceding letters get rearranged

blocks.note: both words taken as written to provide the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Preparations are being arranged ahead of a celebration.
explanation.definitionFit: Easter is the major Christian feast celebrating the resurrection, a principal festival of the church year.

clue.text: Officers heading a cavalry charge?

blocks.note: surface reading: commanders riding at the front of mounted troops
setter's reading: the name is an air force rank, which has nothing to do with horses

explanation.walkthrough: A cavalry squadron does have leaders, but the phrase as a whole is the RAF rank equivalent to a major.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a commissioned rank in the Royal Air Force and other air forces, sitting above flight lieutenant.

clue.text: Prodigal gets a stroke of the whip about six

indicators.note: about means going around, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: a single blow from a whip
six in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: The returning wastrel son is punished with a whipping of half a dozen strokes.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone who spends extravagantly and wastefully, giving freely without restraint.

clue.text: Soubríquet for an airwoman

blocks.note: surface reading: a nickname for a female pilot
setter's reading: a female flier is a woman of rank who flies, so a titled woman plus a winged creature

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer into two words: a titled woman and a creature that flies. It is also the name of a small spotted beetle, and the nickname of Lady Bird Johnson.
explanation.definitionFit: A noblewoman joined to a flying creature makes a fitting nickname for a woman who flies aircraft.

clue.text: State of the huntress' dinner

blocks.note: a meal is what ends up inside the eater
Diana is the Roman goddess of the hunt

explanation.surface: A question about what the goddess of hunting eats for supper.
explanation.walkthrough: The huntress's dinner is whatever is inside Diana, so the clue reads as the phrase 'in Diana'.
explanation.definitionFit: Indiana is one of the fifty United States, in the Midwest, with Indianapolis as its capital.

clue.text: One sees them going right up the Strand!

definitions.text: One sees them going right up the Strand!

blocks.clueFragment: One sees them going right up the Strand!
blocks.note: surface reading: something travelling the length of the famous London street
setter's reading: a strand is a beach, and the sea climbs furthest up it at a particular time

explanation.walkthrough: The capital S points to the Strand, a major street in central London; uncapitalised, a strand is a shore.
explanation.definitionFit: At their peak the sea's twice-daily rise reaches the top of the shore, covering the whole beach.

clue.text: Dangers for those mounting ladders on board

blocks.note: surface reading: hazards for workmen climbing ladders
setter's reading: the ladders are on a game board, where certain squares send a player sliding back down

explanation.walkthrough: The children's board game pairs ladders, which take you up, with creatures that take you down.
explanation.definitionFit: In the classic board game these reptiles are the hazards that send a climbing player back toward the start.

clue.text: Not necessarily a low cur

blocks.note: surface reading: a remark that a mongrel need not be base or contemptible
setter's reading: split the answer and you get a canine placed beneath, though the word usually means a contestant expected to lose

explanation.walkthrough: Read literally the answer is a dog that is underneath; in use it means the side expected to lose, which need not be a dog at all.
explanation.definitionFit: The everyday sense is the competitor given little chance of winning, which is why it is not necessarily any kind of canine.

clue.text: A bit of a pig for drink

definitions.note: the answer is a cask or measure for drink, not the drink itself

blocks.note: first meaning, read as two words: the head belonging to a swine
second meaning: a large cask, or a measure of wine or beer

explanation.surface: Part of a pig is cooked or offered with something to drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A hogshead is a large barrel used for holding ale or wine, and a standard measure of it.

clue.text: A good stroke for 1?

blocks.note: surface reading: a recommended technique for the answer to 1 across
setter's reading: the answer names a swimming style, usually followed by the word stroke

explanation.walkthrough: 1 across refers to people who swim; the answer is one of their standard styles, the one done face down with frog-like kicks.
explanation.definitionFit: The breaststroke is a common swimming technique, so it suits people who swim.

clue.text: Looking back, she was not well

indicators.note: looking back means facing the other way, so the word is read from end to start

blocks.note: to be unwell is to be ailing

explanation.surface: Someone recalls that a woman had been in poor health.
explanation.definitionFit: Delia is a woman's name, so the pronoun stands for any female person by that name.

clue.text: Running buffet?

blocks.note: surface reading: a self-service spread that keeps going all day
setter's reading: the buffet is literally moving, on a train

explanation.walkthrough: Running suggests continuous service; here it means travelling along the rails.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway carriage where meals are served is a restaurant that moves while passengers eat.

clue.text: A visitor would not leave it on Royalty

blocks.clueFragment: A visitor would not leave it on Royalty
blocks.note: surface reading: a caller would not leave a visiting card at the palace
setter's reading: in a pack of cards the king, queen and jack carry royal faces

explanation.walkthrough: Callers once left a visiting card; the clue swaps that for the playing card showing a king, queen or jack.
explanation.definitionFit: A king, queen or jack is a face card bearing a royal portrait in a standard deck.

clue.text: Real chaos in a mixed choir here in Belgium

indicators.note: chaos means disorder, so the word before it is jumbled
mixed means stirred together, so the word after it is jumbled
in places one jumbled piece inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written, to be jumbled
taken as written, to be jumbled

explanation.surface: A singing group in Belgium descends into real disorder.
explanation.definitionFit: Charleroi is a large industrial city in the Hainaut province of southern Belgium.

clue.text: Hardy characters

blocks.note: surface reading: people in the novels of Thomas Hardy
setter's reading: tough, austere people, after the ancient Greek city famed for its stern discipline

explanation.walkthrough: The capital H tempts you toward Thomas Hardy's novels, but it is simply the adjective tough.
explanation.definitionFit: Citizens of ancient Sparta were famous for endurance and austerity, so the name now describes rugged, disciplined people.

clue.text: Where one might feel "on top of the world"?

definitions.text: Where one might feel "on top of the world"?

blocks.clueFragment: Where one might feel "on top of the world"?
blocks.note: surface reading: a place that makes you feel elated
setter's reading: literally standing at the uppermost point of the globe

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom means very happy; read literally it is the northernmost point on Earth, top of the map.
explanation.definitionFit: The planet's northern axis point sits at the top of conventional maps and globes.

clue.text: Singapore's a a t e u cracksman?

definitions.text: a a t e u cracksman

blocks.note: first meaning: Sir Stamford ... founded modern Singapore, and its famous hotel bears his name

blocks.clueFragment: a a t e u cracksman
blocks.note: second meaning: the gentleman safe-breaker of E. W. Hornung's stories, the 'amateur cracksman'; the letters are amateur printed with gaps, apparently a typesetting slip

explanation.surface: Asking whether Singapore has its own celebrated burglar.
explanation.walkthrough: A cracksman is a burglar who cracks safes. Hornung's A. J. Raffles, a cricketer-thief, appeared in The Amateur Cracksman (1899).
explanation.definitionFit: The surname belongs both to Singapore's British founder and to a famous fictional gentleman thief.

clue.text: A Lincolnshire borough has its advantages

indicators.note: the town's name is treated as the word borough with a front part attached, and only that front part is kept

blocks.note: Gainsborough is a market town in Lincolnshire, an English county

explanation.surface: A small English town is said to enjoy certain benefits.
explanation.walkthrough: Gainsborough is a town on the River Trent in Lincolnshire; strip off its 'borough' and what it 'has' is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Gains are profits or benefits obtained, which is what advantages are.

clue.text: Can a rat change colour' Yes, to orange

indicators.note: to change colour is to alter appearance, so the letters take a new form

blocks.note: three words taken as written to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A playful question about whether a rodent can turn a different shade.
explanation.walkthrough: Nacarat is a rare word, so the letters of the fodder and the definition do the work.
explanation.definitionFit: Nacarat is a bright orange-red hue, also a fabric dyed that shade.

clue.text: Champion Hen Trophy'

blocks.note: surface reading: a prize awarded at a poultry show
setter's reading: a trophy is often a cup, and a hen's product sits in a small one at breakfast

explanation.walkthrough: A trophy is often a silver cup; the cup a hen would earn is the one holding a boiled one of her own products.
explanation.definitionFit: The small holder for a boiled breakfast item is jokingly the prize cup a laying hen would win.

clue.text: Not likely to be scared

blocks.note: surface reading: describing a brave person who does not frighten easily
setter's reading: a British exclamation of refusal, meaning certainly not

explanation.walkthrough: In British English the phrase is a colloquial way to say 'certainly not!', as well as literally meaning an absence of fright.
explanation.definitionFit: Said as an exclamation it is an emphatic refusal, just like the scornful 'not likely!'.

clue.text: A more than heavenly plant

indicators.note: more than signals that something extra is added on to the following word

blocks.note: like the beings of heaven
taken as written

explanation.surface: A flower so lovely it surpasses the divine.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as 'heavenly with A more', so the article is tacked onto the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Angelica is an aromatic herb whose candied green stems are used to decorate cakes.

clue.text: Qualified as BA (first part)?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who has passed the first part of an arts degree
setter's reading: the B of BA stands for bachelor, an unmarried man, so the qualification is staying single

explanation.walkthrough: A BA is a Bachelor of Arts; its first part, bachelor, also means an unmarried man.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who abstains from marriage and sexual relations lives as a bachelor, single by vow or choice.

clue.text: Would a "No Smoking" order put some of them out of work?

blocks.clueFragment: Would a "No Smoking" order put some of them out of work?
blocks.note: surface reading: a ban on lighting up would cost jobs in the tobacco trade
setter's reading: smoking is also a way of preserving fish and meat, done by tradesmen who preserve food

explanation.walkthrough: Smoking is one method used by people who preserve bacon, ham or fish, as well as by people who process tobacco leaf.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who preserve meat, fish or tobacco by drying, salting or smoking are known by this trade name.

clue.text: Plants hurriedly

definitions.note: the answer is a verb, goes fast, while the clue word is an adverb

blocks.note: first meaning: marsh plants with hollow stems
second meaning: moves or acts with haste

explanation.walkthrough: Plants can also be read as a verb, someone planting in a hurry, which is the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Rushes are tall waterside grasses, and someone who rushes is going quickly or in a hurry.

clue.text: They have every reason to be fallacious

definitions.text: They have every reason to be fallacious

blocks.clueFragment: They have every reason to be fallacious
blocks.note: surface reading: people with excellent motives for being deceitful
setter's reading: they possess endless reasoning, clever but deliberately misleading arguments

explanation.walkthrough: Having every reason sounds like justification; here it means a stock of plausible arguments used to deceive.
explanation.definitionFit: These ancient Greek teachers of rhetoric became known for persuasive but unsound reasoning used to win debates.
